summary.text: A coral reef is an underwater ecosystem built by colonies of coral polyps held together by calcium carbonate.
Though shallow reefs cover less than 0.1% of the ocean, they are home to at least a quarter of all marine species.
Shallow tropical reefs have declined by 50% since 1950, threatened by excess nutrients, ocean warming and acidification, overfishing and runoff.

items.prompt: Shallow coral reefs cover less than 0.1% of the ocean. About what share of all marine species live on them?

options.label: About 1%
About 5%
At least 25%
Nearly 90%

items.explain: Despite their tiny area, shallow reefs are home to at least a quarter of all marine species.

items.prompt: A snorkeler asks what a coral actually is. What is the right answer?

options.label: A plant that grows a stony stem
An animal related to jellyfish
A mineral that crystallizes in warm water
A kind of seaweed that hardens with age

items.explain: Corals belong to the animal phylum Cnidaria, alongside sea anemones and jellyfish.

items.prompt: A volcanic island ringed by a fringing reef sinks very slowly over a long time. What does the reef become?

options.label: It dies, since coral cannot grow upward
It moves down the slope to deeper water
It stays a fringing reef on the sunken rock
A barrier reef, and finally a ring-shaped atoll

items.explain: Growing upward on older dead coral, the fringing reef becomes a barrier reef, and once the island sinks below sea level an atoll remains.

items.prompt: Corals have built reefs for hundreds of millions of years, yet most living reefs are under 10,000 years old. Why?

options.label: Melting ice raised sea level and flooded continental shelves
Reef-building corals only evolved about 10,000 years ago
The oceans cooled after the last ice age ended
Older reefs were all removed by human fishing

items.explain: Most reefs formed after the Last Glacial Period, when melting ice raised sea level and flooded continental shelves.

items.prompt: Fertilizer runoff from nearby farms pours nitrogen and phosphorus into reef waters. How does this affect the reef?

options.label: It feeds the corals, so reefs grow faster
It harms reefs, which flourish in nutrient-poor water
It has no effect, since corals only eat fish
It cools the water and protects the corals

items.explain: Coral reefs flourish in waters with few nutrients, and excess nitrogen and phosphorus are listed among their threats.

items.prompt: A reef whose corals rely on photosynthesizing partners sinks into deeper water faster than it can grow upward. Why do the corals die?

options.label: Water pressure crushes their skeletons
Deep water is too warm for the polyps
Their partners get too little light to make food
Deep water holds no calcium to build with

items.explain: Corals that rely on zooxanthellae die when the water becomes too deep for their symbionts to photosynthesize, a fate called coral drowning.

beats.hook: Darwin predicted that under each ring-shaped reef's lagoon lies the bedrock of a vanished volcano, and later research backed him.

beats.prompt: Put the stages of Darwin's atoll story in order.

items.label: A fringing reef forms around a volcanic island
The reef becomes a barrier reef enclosing a lagoon
The island sinks below sea level
A roughly circular atoll surrounds a central lagoon

beats.explain: As the island subsides, the fringing reef grows upward into a barrier reef, and once the island is gone an atoll with a central lagoon remains.

beats.prompt: The seafloor under a barrier reef starts sinking much faster than the coral can grow upward. What happens?
beats.explain: A rapidly sinking bottom overwhelms coral growth: corals that rely on zooxanthellae die when the water gets too deep for their partners to photosynthesize.

choices.label: The reef breaks loose and floats upward
choices.feedback: Reefs are built on a base of older, dead coral fixed to the bottom; they do not float.

choices.label: The coral speeds up and keeps pace
choices.feedback: Reefs keep pace only when the land sinks slowly; a fast drop can overwhelm coral growth.

choices.label: The coral drowns and the reef dies
It turns into an atoll right away
choices.feedback: An atoll forms when coral keeps up with the sea level; here it cannot.

beats.prompt: Sort each into where reefs do best or what threatens them.
beats.explain: Reefs thrive in warm, shallow, clear, sunny, agitated, nutrient-poor water, while extra nutrients, acidification and overfishing put them at risk.

beats.prompt: One step in this reasoning is wrong; which?

steps.text: Corals are animals related to jellyfish and sea anemones
Unlike anemones, corals secrete hard carbonate skeletons
Colonies of these polyps, held together by calcium carbonate, form reefs
So a reef is rock that formed with no living help

beats.explain: Reefs are built by living coral polyps whose colonies are held together by calcium carbonate; the rock is made by the animals.

paragraphs.heading: What a coral reef is
paragraphs.text: A coral reef is an underwater ecosystem built by corals. Corals are animals, relatives of sea anemones and jellyfish. Each coral is made of polyps living in colonies, and unlike anemones they produce a hard carbonate skeleton that supports and protects them. Most reefs are built from stony corals, and the colonies of polyps are held together by calcium carbonate.

paragraphs.heading: Crowded with life
paragraphs.text: Shallow reefs are sometimes called the rainforests of the sea. They cover less than 0.1% of the ocean, roughly half the area of France, yet at least a quarter of all marine species live on them, from fish and mollusks to sponges and worms. Reefs flourish in water that holds few nutrients. Most grow best in warm, shallow, clear and sunny water in the tropics, though smaller deep and cold water reefs exist elsewhere.

paragraphs.heading: Old builders, young reefs
paragraphs.text: Corals first built reefs 485 million years ago, early in the Ordovician period. Yet most reefs alive today are under 10,000 years old. They formed after the last ice age, when melting ice raised the sea and flooded the continental shelves. As the water rose, reefs grew upward to keep pace, and reefs that rose too slowly could drown for lack of light.

paragraphs.heading: Darwin's three stages
paragraphs.text: During the voyage of the Beagle, Charles Darwin proposed how ring-shaped reefs called atolls form. First, a fringing reef grows around an extinct volcanic island as the island and seafloor sink. If the land sinks slowly, the reef keeps growing upward on older dead coral and becomes a barrier reef, with a lagoon between reef and land. Once the island sinks below the sea, a roughly circular atoll remains around a central lagoon. Darwin predicted the old volcano would lie under each lagoon, and later research supported him.

paragraphs.heading: A reef under threat
paragraphs.text: Shallow tropical reefs have declined by half since 1950, partly because they are sensitive to the condition of the water. Threats include too much nitrogen and phosphorus, warmer and more acidic oceans, and overfishing. Sunscreen and runoff from harmful land use add to the damage.

paragraphs.heading: What reefs give people
paragraphs.text: Reefs support tourism and fisheries, and they protect shorelines. Estimates of their yearly worth to the world vary enormously, from US$30–375 billion in studies from 1997 and 2003 to US$9.9 trillion in a 2014 estimate.
